title: Why did the USSR collapse in 1991?
subject: histoire
description: On December 25, 1991, the red flag came down from the Kremlin for the last time. How could a superpower of fifteen republics come apart in a matter of months?
author: myra-houser

hero.hook: A failed coup in August, a flag lowered at Christmas: in four months, a superpower vanished.

blocks.text: On **December 25, 1991**, Christmas Day, [[Mikhail Gorbachev]], the president of the Soviet Union, announced his resignation. The next day, the Supreme Soviet, the Union's parliament, voted to dissolve the USSR. The date ranks among the most consequential of the 20th century. It came a little over two years after the fall of the Berlin Wall.

The dissolution gave birth to **fifteen** independent states and hastened the breakup of several former allies of Moscow. With the end of the USSR came the end of the [[Cold War]], which had shaped global geopolitics for more than **forty years**. How could a superpower come apart like this, in a matter of months?

sections.title: From the 1917 revolution to the 1922 Union

blocks.text: In **1917**, Russia, a latecomer to the industrial age, overthrew its tsar and tried to build a new society. Lenin and the [[Bolsheviks]] won the struggle for power. In **1922**, they gathered the country into a new state: the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, the USSR.

blocks.caption: The USSR in 1936, with its eleven union republics of the time: map from the American magazine Soviet Russia Today.

blocks.text: Around Russia, the Union brought together **fourteen** other republics: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania on the Baltic, Ukraine, Belarus and Moldova to the west, Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan in the Caucasus, then Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan in Central Asia.

Its first decades were harsh: the death of Lenin, the rise of **Joseph Stalin**, the Great Famine, then World War II. When the war ended in **1945**, the USSR and its former ally, the United States, entered a competition for military, nuclear, technological and diplomatic advantage.

sections.title: Cold War and Warsaw Pact: the cracks

blocks.text: This rivalry became known as the Cold War. The two superpowers never fought each other directly on the battlefield. But in Afghanistan, El Salvador, Korea, Vietnam and Southern Africa, each poured resources into a local side, hoping that its winner would adopt its political and economic system.

In Europe, the countries of the East aligned with Moscow, often to preserve themselves, and adopted communism. The USSR gathered them into a military alliance, the [[Warsaw Pact]]. Protests broke out nonetheless, as in Czechoslovakia in **1968**. Starting in Poland in **1980**, people rose up against the communist parties and Soviet influence. In **1989**, the Warsaw Pact countries cast off their leaders: this was the fall of communism.

sections.title: Glasnost, perestroika and the August 1991 coup

blocks.text: Moscow too was looking for a way out. In **1985**, Mikhail Gorbachev took charge of the country to revive an exhausted Union. Convinced that the public was ready for change, he launched two policies: [[glasnost]], openness, and [[perestroika]], the restructuring of the economy and the state.

blocks.caption: Mikhail Gorbachev in bronze, alongside George Bush and Helmut Kohl: the "Fathers of Unity" monument in Berlin.

blocks.text: The opening released forces the Kremlin could no longer control. Republics long at odds with one another and with Moscow began to break away. Estonia declared its sovereignty in **1988**, Lithuania its independence in **1990**: they were the first to leave. In **August 1991**, party hardliners tried to overthrow Gorbachev.

The coup failed: the plotters never managed to seize power. But it further weakened the alliances inside the Kremlin and exposed the decay of Soviet power structures for all to see. In the chaos of the following months, several more republics declared their independence.

Soviet leaders then negotiated the end of the Union. On **December 21, 1991**, they signed the [[Alma-Ata Protocol]], which designated Russia as the successor to the USSR. Gorbachev's resignation on December 25 transferred power to [[Boris Yeltsin]], the president of Russia. That evening, the Soviet flag flew over the Kremlin for the last time, before the Russian flag replaced it.

blocks.caption: Leonid Kravchuk, Nursultan Nazarbayev, Boris Yeltsin and Stanislav Shushkevich after signing the Alma-Ata Protocol, December 21, 1991.

blocks.text: The Supreme Soviet's vote the next day put an end to **sixty-nine years** of history. Fifteen independent states replaced the Union, with Russia in the lead. Several former allies of Moscow, Czechoslovakia for one, broke apart in their turn. A two-bloc world built around the rivalry between Washington and Moscow faded away in a few months.

The dissolution was voted on December 26, just in time for New Year's Eve, the biggest holiday of the year in the Soviet Union. The country entered 1992 with no USSR, no communist regime and no Cold War.

blocks.text: Born in 1922 out of the Bolshevik revolution, the USSR collapsed in 1991 under an opening it could no longer control, republics breaking away and a failed coup, and its disappearance brought the Cold War to an end.
